Tropical forest trees with alternate simple leaves, resin, five-part flowers and usually a one-seeded nut surrounded by enlarged persistent sepals that can form wings.

New Zealand wineberry
Aristotelia serrata
wineberry; makomako

A deciduous New Zealand tree, often multi-stemmed, with opposite thin leaves and sharply toothed margins. Small unisexual flowers are borne in axillary clusters; male and female flowers usually occur on separate plants. Female plants produce rounded red to dark berries. The paired leaf arrangement and berry clusters distinguish it from many similar shrubs.
Endemic to New Zealand, in forest margins, clearings and regenerating sites from lowlands into montane areas.
Small deciduous tree with opposite branches and a loose rounded crown.
Opposite, thin ovate leaves with a pointed tip and sharply serrated edge.
Small pale unisexual flowers in axillary clusters; sexes are generally on separate trees.
Fleshy red to dark berry containing several seeds, borne on female plants.
Ritter’s cactus
Aztekium ritteri
Ritter’s Aztekium

A minute, slow-growing cactus of northeastern Mexico, typically solitary and only a few centimetres wide. Its grey-green globose stem has many narrow ribs crossed by transverse grooves, giving it a distinctly wrinkled surface. Tiny areoles carry short bristles; small pale pink flowers arise near the crown. This compact, ribbed body is unlike the columnar or pad-forming cacti.
Restricted to limestone cliffs and rocky slopes in northeastern Mexico, especially Nuevo León.
Very small, usually solitary globose cactus with closely spaced, transversely grooved ribs.
True leaves are absent; short bristles arise from tiny areoles on the ribs.
Small pale pink flower near the stem apex, with numerous stamens.
Small fleshy fruit containing dark seeds.
Bidi-leaf bauhinia
Bauhinia racemosa
Bidi-leaf tree; aapta

A small deciduous tree or large shrub of seasonally dry South Asian habitats. Its simple alternate leaves are divided at the tip into two rounded lobes, like a camel’s hoof. Racemes carry small pale flowers with five unequal petals and long stamens; mature fruit is a flat, elongated legume. The leaf is one blade with a deep notch, not two separate leaflets.
Native from the Indian subcontinent through parts of Indochina to Yunnan; common in dry woodland and scrub.
Small branched deciduous tree or shrub with a light crown.
Alternate simple blade divided apically into two rounded lobes.
Small pale yellow-green flower with five petals and conspicuous stamens.
Flattened brown legume that opens along its sutures.
Nodding bur-marigold
Bidens cernua
nodding beggar-ticks

An annual of wet shores and marsh edges, with erect stems and opposite, toothed leaves. Yellow composite flower heads often nod; their apparent single flowers are actually many disk florets surrounded by ray florets. The narrow dry fruits have barbed awns that cling to fur and clothing. It is distinguished from many Bidens by its nodding heads and wetland habitat.
Widespread in temperate and subarctic regions of the Northern Hemisphere, especially in shallow-water margins and wet ground.
Erect annual wetland herb with branching flowering stems.
Opposite lance-shaped leaves with serrated edges, often partly clasping the stem.
Nodding yellow head of many florets, with yellow ray florets at the margin.
Narrow dark achene with barbed awns for attachment to animals.
Large quaking-grass
Briza maxima
greater quaking grass; big quaking grass

A delicate annual grass native to Mediterranean and Macaronesian regions. Slender stems carry loose, open panicles whose conspicuous, flattened, heart-shaped spikelets hang on fine stalks and tremble in the wind. Each spikelet contains several overlapping florets; the mature grass fruit is a small grain. The large dangling spikelets distinguish it from finer grasses and from the smaller spikelets of Briza media.
Native to Macaronesia and the Mediterranean region; introduced and naturalised in many other temperate and subtropical areas.
Loosely tufted annual with slender upright culms and open panicles.
Narrow flat grass blades with a membranous ligule at the sheath junction.
Loose panicle of large, pendulous, flattened spikelets with heart-shaped outlines.
Small grain (caryopsis) enclosed within a mature floret.
Taiwan incense cedar
Chamaecyparis formosensis
Formosan cypress; Taiwan cypress

A very tall evergreen conifer endemic to Taiwan’s montane forests. Flattened branch sprays carry tiny opposite scale leaves, and the fibrous reddish-brown bark breaks into long strips. Small rounded seed cones mature on the branchlets; separate pollen cones produce pollen. It is a true cypress, not a pine, and is assessed as Endangered in the IUCN data surfaced by Kew.
Endemic to central and northern Taiwan, chiefly in cool, moist montane forest.
Tall evergreen tree with a straight trunk, conical crown and fibrous bark.
Flattened sprays of tiny scale-like leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Separate inconspicuous pollen cones and seed cones; no petals.
Small rounded woody seed cone that opens by several shield-like scales.
Red-flowered combretum
Combretum paniculatum
flame creeper; red combretum

A woody African scrambling climber with opposite, simple leaves and showy terminal or axillary panicles of scarlet flowers. The tubular flowers have a small four- or five-lobed limb; after flowering, dry fruits develop with wing-like angles characteristic of Combretum. It climbs through surrounding vegetation rather than forming a self-supporting tree crown.
Tropical Africa south to the Limpopo region, in woodland, thickets and forest margins.
Woody scrambling climber with long flexible stems that lean on neighbouring plants.
Opposite, entire, elliptic leaves with a pointed tip and clear lateral veins.
Dense terminal panicles of small tubular scarlet-red flowers.
Dry, winged, indehiscent fruit; the wings aid dispersal.
Teddy-bear cholla
Cylindropuntia bigelovii
teddy-bear cactus; jumping cholla

A branching desert cactus with cylindrical, jointed stems densely clothed in pale spines. The spines emerge from areoles and are enclosed in papery sheaths; stem joints detach readily and can attach to passing animals. Yellow-green flowers arise at the branch tips, followed by spiny fleshy fruits. Despite its soft-looking coat, it is highly spiny and should not be handled.
Native to arid regions from southern Nevada and Arizona to New Mexico and northwestern Mexico.
Dense branching shrub of upright cylindrical segments that readily detach.
True leaves are minute and short-lived; conspicuous spines arise from areoles on the stems.
Yellow-green flower at the tip of a stem segment.
Spiny green fleshy fruit, often persisting on the plant.
Desert Christmas cactus
Cylindropuntia leptocaulis
Christmas cholla; pencil cholla

A finely branched desert cactus with very slender cylindrical green stems and widely spaced areoles. Its tiny leaves are fleeting, while the spines are usually shorter and less dense than those of teddy-bear cholla. Small pale flowers appear in spring; conspicuous smooth red fruits often remain through winter and give the common name its seasonal association.
Native from Oklahoma and Texas into northern and central Mexico, in dry scrub and desert margins.
Open, intricately branched shrub with thin pencil-like cylindrical stems.
Tiny, short-lived leaves may appear on young growth; areoles bear few short spines.
Small pale yellow-green flower arising from a stem tip.
Smooth, round red fruit, commonly persistent on the stems.
Cheddar pink
Dianthus gratianopolitanus
clove pink; grey pink

A low evergreen perennial forming dense cushions of narrow blue-grey leaves. Its upright stems carry fragrant pink flowers with five petals cut into fine teeth or fringes; the tubular calyx is surrounded by small bracts. A dry capsule opens at maturity. The compact mat and deeply fringed petals distinguish this species from taller garden carnations.
Native to central and western Europe, often on dry calcareous rocks and short turf.
Low evergreen cushion with short flowering stems above a dense mat of foliage.
Narrow blue-grey leaves, opposite and joined at the base.
Pink five-petalled flower with a deeply fringed margin and tubular calyx.
Dry cylindrical capsule opening at its apex to release seeds.
Resin-tree dipterocarp
Dipterocarpus alatus
yang; canarium tree

A large evergreen Southeast Asian rainforest tree with a straight trunk, broad crown and often buttressed base. Alternate leathery leaves have a prominent midrib and many parallel secondary veins. Five-petalled flowers are borne in clusters. The one-seeded nut is surrounded by persistent sepals, two of which enlarge into long wings; this winged fruit is characteristic of the genus.
Native from northeastern India through mainland Southeast Asia to Peninsular Malaysia and Luzon; associated with moist tropical forest.
Tall emergent evergreen tree with a straight bole and flared buttresses.
Large alternate simple leaf with entire margin and prominent pinnate venation.
Small fragrant flower with five pale petals and numerous stamens.
Single nut with two greatly enlarged wing-like sepals and three shorter lobes.
Braun’s dragon tree
Dracaena braunii
Braun’s dracaena; central African dracaena

A small perennial or subshrub of Central African forests. It has slender woody canes and narrow lance-shaped leaves, which can vary in stalk length and gather toward shoot tips. Small flowers are grouped in a branched inflorescence, followed by orange-red berries. It is taxonomically distinct from Dracaena sanderiana, the species commonly sold as “lucky bamboo”; the shared trade name is misleading.
Native to Cameroon, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon and the Republic of the Congo, in western Central African tropical forest.
Small branched perennial or subshrub with slender cane-like shoots.
Narrow lance-shaped leaves borne along the shoots and gathered toward their ends.
Small pale flowers grouped in a branched inflorescence.
Orange-red berry following flowering.
Guanacaste tree
Enterolobium cyclocarpum
ear tree; elephant-ear tree; conacaste

A large tropical American tree known for its exceptionally broad spreading crown. Its leaves are twice pinnate, with many tiny leaflets; spherical heads of numerous small pale flowers appear on the branches. The distinctive thick, dark pod curls into a nearly closed ear-shaped ring. The leaves and coiled fruit together make the species easy to recognise.
Native from Mexico through Central America into northern South America; cultivated widely in tropical regions.
Massive deciduous tree with a wide umbrella-shaped crown and spreading limbs.
Bipinnate leaf divided into many small opposite leaflets.
Spherical head of numerous small greenish-white flowers.
Thick dark legume that curves into a closed or nearly closed ring.
Abd al Kuri spurge
Euphorbia abdelkuri
Abdel Kuri euphorbia

A distinctive succulent shrub endemic to the small island of Abd al Kuri, off Socotra. Its pale grey-green, leafless stems branch from a short woody base and store water; the stems are angular or faintly ribbed but lack cactus areoles. Tiny cyathia, the specialised flower clusters of Euphorbia, form near the branch tips and produce three-lobed capsules. It is an unusual spurge, not a cactus.
Restricted to Abd al Kuri Island in the Socotra Archipelago, Yemen, in arid rocky habitats.
Compact succulent shrub with a basal trunk and many upright pale stems.
Leaves are absent or extremely reduced; photosynthesis takes place in the fleshy stems.
Tiny yellow-green cyathium, a cup-like inflorescence unique to Euphorbia.
Three-lobed dry capsule produced by the cyathium.
Tartary buckwheat
Fagopyrum tataricum
bitter buckwheat; Tatar buckwheat

An annual crop related to sorrels and knotweeds, not a true cereal grass. Its alternate leaves have a broad heart-shaped base, while small greenish-white flowers grow in clusters. The dry fruit is a three-angled achene; the edible seed is used as a pseudocereal. Compared with common buckwheat, Tartary buckwheat is generally more bitter and often retains its hull closely around the grain.
Originating in Tibet and central China; cultivated across parts of Asia and elsewhere in cool temperate regions.
Annual branching herb with slender stems and small clustered flowers.
Alternate triangular to heart-shaped leaves with a pointed apex and sheathing stipules at nodes.
Small greenish-white five-part flowers in axillary or terminal clusters.
Three-angled dry achene containing the edible seed.
Sea rush
Juncus maritimus
maritime rush

A robust perennial rush of salt marshes, coastal flats and brackish wetlands. Tough cylindrical leaves and stems rise from creeping rhizomes. Its compact brown flower clusters appear lateral because a long, sharp bract continues beyond them as if it were the stem tip. Each tiny flower has six tepals; a dry capsule forms later. Solid round stems help distinguish rushes from many grasses, whose stems are typically hollow and jointed.
Native across Macaronesia, Europe, North Africa and parts of western and central Asia; chiefly coastal and saline wetlands.
Dense perennial tussock spreading by rhizomes in salt marshes and wet coastal ground.
Stiff, narrow, cylindrical leaves arise mostly from the base.
Small brown clusters of six-tepalled flowers appear beside a long continuation bract.
Dry many-seeded capsule with three valves.
White-wicky
Kalmia cuneata
white wicky; white-wickery

A deciduous shrub of wet savannas and bog margins in the Carolinas. Its alternate leaves are narrow at the base and broaden toward the tip; small terminal clusters bear creamy white flowers with a red band inside. Ten stamens are held under tension in pockets of the saucer-shaped corolla and spring forward when released, a useful Kalmia character. A dry capsule follows.
Endemic to the coastal plain of North and South Carolina, USA, in wet acidic habitats.
Spreading to upright deciduous shrub, usually under 1.5 m tall.
Alternate oblanceolate leaves, widest near the tip and tapering to a narrow base.
Creamy white saucer-shaped flower with a red inner band and ten pocketed stamens.
Small dry capsule opening at maturity.
Common liverwort
Marchantia polymorpha
umbrella liverwort; Marchantia

A thalloid liverwort whose visible green body is the dominant gametophyte, not a leafy stemmed plant. Flat branching ribbons grow as low rosettes on damp soil or rock. The upper surface has air pores and toothed gemma cups containing disc-shaped propagules; scales and rhizoids occupy the underside. Female plants raise umbrella-like archegoniophores, while separate male plants form flatter antheridiophores. Its capsules release spores, but gemmae also allow rapid clonal spread.
Nearly cosmopolitan on moist soil, rock, banks and greenhouse surfaces.
Low, flat, dichotomously branching thallus forming a green mat or rosette.
Leaves are absent; the dorsal thallus has air pores and gemma cups, while rhizoids and scales are ventral.
Flowers are absent; separate male and female plants bear stalked antheridiophores or umbrella-like archegoniophores.
A short-lived sporophyte forms a capsule beneath the female receptacle and releases spores.
Texas rainbow cactus
Echinocereus dasyacanthus
strawberry cactus; rainbow hedgehog cactus

A low, usually clustering cactus of the Chihuahuan Desert region. Its short cylindrical stems have multiple ribs bearing evenly spaced areoles with many radial spines. Large funnel-shaped flowers open near the stem tips; the species is notable for colour variation, though yellow is common. Smooth fleshy fruits develop after flowering. The cylindrical clustered stems distinguish it from globular cacti and tall columnar forms.
Native to southern New Mexico and western Texas, extending into northern Mexico, especially dry rocky grassland and desert scrub.
Low clump of short, stout, ribbed cylindrical stems.
True leaves are absent; dense spines emerge from areoles along the stem ribs.
Large funnel-shaped flower with many yellow tepals and numerous stamens.
Fleshy green to reddish fruit, often spiny when young.
Phillip Island hibiscus
Hibiscus insularis
Philip Island hibiscus

A rare shrub naturally confined to Phillip Island south of Norfolk Island. Its leaves are alternate and may be shallowly lobed; the large hibiscus flowers open cream to pale green with a dark magenta centre, then redden as they age. A central staminal column carries the fused stamens. The island’s wild population is extremely restricted, although plantings now occur more widely on Norfolk Island.
Endemic in the wild to Phillip Island, Norfolk Island group, southwest Pacific; widely planted on Norfolk Island for conservation.
Upright woody shrub with several branches and alternate foliage.
Alternate ovate leaves, sometimes shallowly lobed, with toothed margins.
Large five-petalled flower, initially cream-green with a dark magenta centre; petals redden with age.
Dry five-valved capsule developing inside the persistent calyx.
